# Subhāsita Sutta (Snp 3.3 (PTS Snp 78))

**ID:** Snp 3.3 (PTS Snp 78)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Subhāsita Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Subhāsita Sutta* ("Well-Spoken Words", also translated as "Good Words") is the third discourse of the Mahāvagga in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 3.3, PTS Snp 78–79) [Catalog; Norman 1997-2001; Saddhatissa 2013; Seyfort Ruegg 2010]. Set at Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery in the Jeta Grove near Sāvatthi, the Buddha addresses the monks on the four qualities that constitute blameless, well-spoken speech (*subhāsita*) that is not censured by the wise [Hazra 1994; Saddhatissa 2013]. According to the sutta, a monk should utter speech that is well-spoken rather than ill-spoken, pleasing rather than unpleasing, right or beneficial rather than unrighteous, and true rather than untrue [Hazra 1994; Saddhatissa 2013].

Structurally, the discourse consists of introductory prose followed by verses, with prose intervening between the opening statement and additional stanzas ascribed to the venerable Vaṅgīsa [Katre 1931; Saddhatissa 2013]. The poetic portion celebrates truth as the "voice of the immortal" and praises wholesome speech that leads to peace [Dhammapala et al. 1984; Rotman 2013]. In the commentarial literature, the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* (SnA 394) specifically comments on the text's canonical prose introduction [Balasooriya et al. 1980].

 Four of the sutta's stanzas are directly identical with verses preserved under Vaṅgīsa's name in the *Theragāthā* (Thag 1227–1230 in Thag 21.1) and are also aligned with the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus; Katre 1931]. Furthermore, passage-level parallels and DharmaNexus alignments link its verses to the *Vācavarga* / Speech chapters of the Sanskrit, Tibetan, and Chinese *Udānavarga* collections (UV 8; D0326; T 210.8, T 210.38, T 212.9, T 213.8), the *Śarīrārthagāthā*, and citations in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 3) [DharmaNexus].
